extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students of humor theory, cognitive scientists, philosophers of emotion
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical account of humor that models affective interpretations of situations using two predicates — Violation (V) and Normality (N) — and classifies humor into three levels based on their combination. The page explains logical issues and proposes how to represent N and V as predicates over different aspects of situations or as uncertain inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: No violation (Level 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: No violation occurs when there is no perceived violation (¬V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level 1 is the category where the situation is perceived as NOT a violation. This is the baseline, non-humorous interpretation when no violation is detected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funny violation (Level 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A funny violation occurs when a perceived violation is juxtaposed with a simultaneous view of the situation as normal (V ∧ N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level 2 arises when the observer holds two affective interpretations at once: that part/aspect of the situation is a violation, while another perspective treats it as normal. This juxtaposition (V combined with N) is the core condition for humor in this model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive violation (Level 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive violation occurs when there is a perceived violation but there is no competing view of the situation as normal, or where the competing view is driven out by the strength of affective commitment to the principle being violated (V ∧ ¬N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level 3 is when the violation dominates interpretation (no balancing normal view) and thus elicits offense rather than amusement; strong affective commitment to the violated principle suppresses any normalizing perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating N and V as simple, mutually exclusive atomic propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: If N and V are treated as elementary propositions with definite, mutually exclusive truth values then N ∧ V is logically inconsistent, producing an apparent paradox for situations that seem both normal and violating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against modeling N and V as direct negations of each other (¬V = N, ¬N = V) at the atomic level because real situations can appear to be both normal and violating in different respects; doing so creates logical inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model N and V as predicates over different proposition-sets (N(p1), V(p2))
rubrics_metrics.description: N and V are predicates with limited scope over specific aspects of complex situations, e.g. N(p1) and V(p2). If p1 and p2 are distinct (though perhaps overlapping) sets of propositions, then N(p1) ∧ V(p2) is logically consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent different 'views of the same situation' as applying to different elements/aspects. This argument-structure approach allows the same overall situation to yield both normal and violating affective interpretations without logical contradiction. Example notation and explanation are provided (N(p1), V(p2)). The author favors this approach because it makes stronger empirical claims and requires fewer assumptions about human reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow affective inferences to be probabilistic/uncertain rather than logically definite
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional inferences from apparent facts may be made by rules of likelihood or probable association rather than by logical necessity; the mind can consider inconsistent inferences without attaching definite truth values to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humans may hold uncertain or tentative affective interpretations; the mind can 'consider' conflicting inferences (e.g., one reading treating something as normal, another as a violation) without committing to both as definitely true. This probabilistic treatment resolves apparent logical contradictions and explains affective 'absurdity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of coexisting N and V interpretations: ambiguity, temporal sequencing, complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Different aspects of a complex situation can lead to contrary emotional interpretations through ambiguity, temporal sequencing, or mere complexity in the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page identifies mechanisms by which a situation yields N(p1) and V(p2): ambiguity in which aspect is attended, sequencing of perspectives over time, and the inherent complexity of situations. These mechanisms explain how affective 'absurdity' (simultaneous impressions of normality and violation) arises and is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for the predicate-over-aspects approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the two approaches to resolving the N∧V paradox (argument-structure/predicate approach vs. probabilistic inference), the author prefers treating N and V as predicates over different proposition-sets because it 'makes stronger empirical claims, and requires fewer assumptions about human reasoning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling humorous interpretation, favor the explanation that different perspectives apply to different factual aspects (N(p1), V(p2)) unless empirical cases show this approach inapplicable. This is recommended as the working assumption in the text.
